editorial:
When you meet Juli Baker in second grade, she already knows Bryce Loski is the one. The problem? Bryce thinks she's just the weird girl who won't leave him alone. Told from both sides of the story, this sweet coming-of-age romance flips between their viewpoints as six years pass. You watch Juli chase Bryce, then finally give up, right as Bryce starts to see what he's been missing. Set in the early 1960s, the movie has a warm, nostalgic feel that pulls you in from the start.

The young cast does a wonderful job, and Rob Reiner's gentle direction keeps things heartfelt without getting too cheesy. You'll love the dual perspective gimmick, the sycamore tree storyline, and the way both families feel real. On the downside, the pacing can feel slow in spots, and the ending is a bit predictable. If you enjoy tender, old-fashioned love stories, this one is for you.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, Bryce finally understands Juli's worth after his grandfather points out her character. He realizes his own family's flaws and how unfairly he treated her. Bryce buys a young sycamore tree, the same kind Juli loved that was cut down, and plants it in her yard. Juli sees him working and comes outside. They share a quiet, hopeful moment together, suggesting their relationship is just beginning. It's a sweet, open-ended conclusion that leaves you smiling.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves sweet coming-of-age romances.
